29	mask: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = mat(blockSize, blockSize, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => if j > i then -(10.0^10) else 0.0 end)
30	rmsn_b(dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
31	    r = SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|); y = x / r
32	    (dy - y ((y DOT dy) / |y|)) / r
33	  end
34	sm_b(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = p × (dy - (p DOT dy))
35	
36	(* ------------------------------- tactic 2/8: one vector, nine views ------ *)
37	matName(i: ZZ32): String =
38	    if i = 0 then "wte" elif i = 1 then "wpe" elif i = 2 then "lm_head" elif i = 3 then "attn_wq" elif i = 4 then "attn_wk"
39	    elif i = 5 then "attn_wv" elif i = 6 then "attn_wo" elif i = 7 then "mlp_fc1" else "mlp_fc2" end
40	matShape(i: ZZ32): (ZZ32, ZZ32) =
41	    if (i = 0) OR (i = 2) then (vocabSize, nEmbd) elif i = 7 then (4 nEmbd, nEmbd) elif i = 8 then (nEmbd, 4 nEmbd) else (nEmbd, nEmbd) end
42	matCount(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (r, c) = matShape(i); r c end
43	matOffset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] matCount(j)
44	nParams(): ZZ32 = matOffset(9)
45	view(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do (r, c) = matShape(i); view(p, matOffset(i), r, c) end
46	
47	(* -------------------- tactic 3/5: the corpus as one padded integer matrix - *)
48	corpus: Corpus = loadCorpus(corpusPath, blockSize, bosId)
49	
50	(* ------------------------- the step: keys -> (loss, flat gradient). Pure. -- *)
51	step(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): (RR64, Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
52	    ids = corpus.tokens(b, 0); tg = corpus.tokens(b, 1); vm = corpus.valid(b); nv = SUM vm; pos = corpus.positions(b)
53	    (wte, wpe, lm, wq, wk, wv, wo, f1, f2) = (view(p, 0), view(p, 1), view(p, 2), view(p, 3), view(p, 4), view(p, 5), view(p, 6), view(p, 7), view(p, 8))
54	    h(m: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = heads(m, blockSize, nHead, headDim)
55	    u(t: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = unheads(t, nHead)
56	    (* -- forward, all (doc, pos) rows at once -- *)
57	    x = gather(wte, ids) + gather(wpe, pos); xp = rows(rmsn, x); x1 = rows(rmsn, xp)
58	    (q, k, v) = (x1 wq^T, x1 wk^T, x1 wv^T); (qh, kh, vh) = (h(q), h(k), h(v))
59	    a = rows(sm, mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)); hc = u(a vh)
60	    x2 = xp + hc wo^T; x3 = rows(rmsn, x2); m0 = x3 f1^T; mr = 0.0 MAX m0; x4 = x2 + mr f2^T
61	    pr = rows(sm, x4 lm^T); loss = -(vm DOT log(pick(pr, tg))) / nv
62	    (* -- backward, one line under each forward line, bottom-up -- *)
63	    dL = diag(vm / nv) (pr - onehot(tg, vocabSize)); gLM = dL^T x4; dX4 = dL lm
64	    gF2 = dX4^T mr; dM0 = (dX4 f2) × (m0 > 0.0); gF1 = dM0^T x3; dX3 = dM0 f1
65	    dX2 = dX4 + rows(rmsn_b, dX3, x2); gWO = dX2^T hc; dh = h(dX2 wo)
66	    dVh = a^T dh; dS = rows(sm_b, a, dh vh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)
67	    dQh = dS kh; dKh = dS^T qh; (dQ, dK, dV) = (u(dQh), u(dKh), u(dVh))
68	    (gWQ, gWK, gWV) = (dQ^T x1, dK^T x1, dV^T x1); dX1 = dQ wq + dK wk + dV wv
69	    dXp = dX2 + rows(rmsn_b, dX1, xp); dX = rows(rmsn_b, dXp, x)
70	    gWTE = transpose(onehot(ids, vocabSize)) dX; gWPE = transpose(onehot(pos, blockSize)) dX
71	    (loss, flat(gWTE, gWPE, gLM, gWQ, gWK, gWV, gWO, gF1, gF2))
72	  end
73	
74	(* --------------------- Adam: three whole-vector expressions over p, m, v -- *)
75	adam(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], g: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], t: ZZ32, lr: RR64):
76	    (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
77	    m' = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) g
78	    v' = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) (g × g)
79	    p' = p - (lr (m' / (1 - beta1^t))) / (SQRT (v' / (1 - beta2^t)) + epsilon_A)
80	    (p', m', v')
81	  end
82	learningRate(s: ZZ32): RR64 = lr0 (1 - (1.0 s) / nSteps)
83	
84	(* --------------------------------------------------- training ----------- *)
85	run(): () = do
86	    println "microgpt flat | params " nParams() " | corpus " corpus.size() " x " (blockSize + 1) " | batch 1, 5 steps"
87	    bsz = 1
88	    p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := loadParams(weightsDir, matName, 9, nParams())
89	    m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
90	    v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
91	    for s <- seq(0#5) do
92	        t0 = nanoTime()
93	        (l, g) = step(p, keys(bsz, fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => (s bsz + i) MOD corpus.size()))
94	        (p, m, v) := adam(p, m, v, g, s + 1, learningRate(s))
95	        println "step " (s + 1) " loss " l "  (" ((nanoTime() - t0) DIV 1000000) " ms)"
96	    end
97	  end
98	end

(* FlatArrays -- the array vocabulary of Run C4: what the shipped
   Vector/Matrix algebra lacks, declared once in the library's own style over
   the library's own arrays.  Round two's vocabulary (explorations/run-c/src)
   less the block, ravel, vector-gather and validity pieces that the corpus
   object of FlatData makes unnecessary; the inventory it was built against
   is round three's survey (explorations/run-c3/survey.md).  Views take their
   shapes at run time through the library's own reflect idiom
   (FortressLibrary.fss:1922-1934). *)
component FlatArrays
export FlatArrays
import NatReflect.{...}

(* ------------------------------------------------------- constructors ---- *)
vec(n: ZZ32, f: ZZ32 -> RR64): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).tabulate(f)
zeros(n: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).fill(0.0)
keys(n: ZZ32, f: ZZ32 -> ZZ32): Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\] = array[\ZZ32\](n).tabulate(f)
mat(r: ZZ32, c: ZZ32, f: (ZZ32,ZZ32) -> RR64): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = array[\RR64\](r,c).tabulate(f)

(* ------------------------------------------- the elementwise algebra ----- *)
(* One declaration per operator, generic in the index type I, so a vector
   (I = ZZ32), a matrix ((ZZ32,ZZ32)) and a rank-3 array share it.  A scalar
   times an array is the library's juxtaposition and is not redeclared;
   + and - between two arrays of one shape, and + - MIN MAX between an array
   and a scalar, are the library's. *)
opr ×[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], b: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (i: I, e: RR64): RR64 => e b[i])
opr /[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], b: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (i: I, e: RR64): RR64 => e / b[i])
opr /[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => e / s)
(* a comparison on an array is a 0/1 array *)
opr >[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\], s: RR64): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => if e > s then 1.0 else 0.0 end)
opr SQRT[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => SQRT e)
exp[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => exp(e))
log[\I\](a: Array[\RR64,I\]): Array[\RR64,I\] = a.map[\RR64\](fn (e: RR64): RR64 => log(e))
(* diag(v) m scales the rows of m: the Dyalog's v ×⍤0 1 m.  A diagonal is a
   read-only Matrix view; the library's product forwards to its mul, which
   scales the rows without forming the matrix. *)
object Diag[\nat s\](d: Vector[\RR64,s\]) extends Matrix[\RR64,s,s\]
    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; if i = j then d[i] else 0.0 end end
    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = fail("a diagonal is read-only")
    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = fail("a diagonal is read-only")
    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,s,0,s\] = array2[\U,s,s\]()
    mul[\nat s2\](other: Matrix[\RR64,s,s2\]): Matrix[\RR64,s,s2\] =
        other.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), e: RR64): RR64 => do (i, j) = ij; d[i] e end)
end
diag[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\]): Diag[\s\] = Diag[\s\](v)

(* ----------------------------------------------------- transposes -------- *)
(* as functions: an API cannot declare a postfix operator (ledger row 133), so
   the model declares ^T itself over these; and a call result may not be
   followed by ^T at all (rows 144, 158) *)
transpose[\nat r, nat c\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Matrix[\RR64,c,r\] = m.t()
transpose[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]): Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = Transposed3[\a,b,c\](t)

(* ------------------------------------------------------------ views ----- *)
(* the (nr x nc) matrix at off in a flat vector, row-major *)
object PView[\nat s, nat r, nat c\](base: Vector[\RR64,s\], off: ZZ32) extends Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]
    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; base.get(off + i c + j) end
    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.put(off + i c + j, x) end
    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.init0(off + i c + j, x) end
    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,r,0,c\] = array2[\U,r,c\]()
end

93	heads[\nat br, nat bc\](base: Matrix[\RR64,br,bc\], p: ZZ32, nh: ZZ32, k: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do

100	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.put(((i DIV b) nh + (j DIV c), i MOD b, j MOD c), x) end
101	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.init0(((i DIV b) nh + (j DIV c), i MOD b, j MOD c), x) end
102	    replica[\U\](): Array2[\U,0,r,0,cc\] = array2[\U,r,cc\]()
103	end

105	    UnheadsView[\a,b,c,r,cc\](base, nh)
106	unheads[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], nh: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do

110	(* a plane of a rank-3 array as a matrix, and every plane transposed *)
111	object PlaneView[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], p: ZZ32) extends Matrix[\RR64,b,c\]
112	    get(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (i, j) = ij; base.get((p, i, j)) end
113	    put(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.put((p, i, j), x) end
114	    init0(ij: (ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (i, j) = ij; base.init0((p, i, j), x) end

118	object Transposed3[\nat a, nat b, nat c\](base: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\]) extends Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\]
119	    get(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)): RR64 = do (p, i, j) = ix; base.get((p, j, i)) end
120	    put(ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), x: RR64): () = do (p, i, j) = ix; base.put((p, j, i), x) end

126	(* +.×⍤2 : the library product on every pair of planes *)
127	opr juxtaposition[\nat a, nat b, nat c, nat a2, nat b2, nat c2\](x: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\], y: Array3[\RR64,0,a2,0,b2,0,c2\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
128	    (np, n, d) = x.sizes
129	    (yp, yn, yd) = y.sizes
130	    out = array[\RR64\](np, n, yd)
131	    for p <- 0#np do (plane(out, p)).assign((plane(x, p)) (plane(y, p))) end
132	    out
133	  end

135	opr +[\nat r, nat c, nat a, nat b, nat d\](m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\], t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,d\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
136	    t.ivmap[\RR64\](fn (ix: (ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32), e: RR64): RR64 => do (p, i, j) = ix; m[i,j] + e end)
137

140	   rows of two matrices; over a rank-3 array the rows are those of every plane.
141	   A parallel for over the rows, each written through a row view. *)
142	rows[\nat r, nat c\](f: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] -> Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do
143	    (n, d) = m.sizes
144	    out = array[\RR64\](n, d)

146	    out

155	    (np, n, d) = t.sizes
156	    out = array[\RR64\](np, n, d)

1	(* FlatData -- the loaders and the corpus for MicroGptFlat (Run C4).
2	   The weights are nine text files, one matrix row per line, read straight
3	   into one flat vector in layout order; the corpus is one padded integer
4	   matrix (documents x block+1) with a length per document (Hsu's tactics
5	   3 and 5). The float parser is here because the library's strToFloat
6	   mis-parses a sign and overflows on a 17-digit mantissa (ledger row 140)
7	   and String.split is not a tokenizer (row 141). *)
8	component FlatData
9	export FlatData
10	import FlatArrays.{...}
11	import File.{...}
12	
13	(* decimal digits, optional '.', optional e/E exponent; leading '-' or '¯' *)
14	parseFloat(s: String): RR64 = do
15	    neg = (s[0] = '-') OR (s[0] = '¯')
16	    m: RR64 := 0.0
17	    scale: ZZ32 := 0
18	    ex: ZZ32 := 0
19	    i: ZZ32 := if neg then 1 else 0 end
20	    seenPoint: Boolean := false
21	    n = |s|
22	    while (i < n) AND: ((s[i] =/= 'e') AND (s[i] =/= 'E')) do
23	        c = s[i]
24	        if c = '.' then seenPoint := true
25	        else
26	            m := 10.0 m + (c.codePoint - '0'.codePoint)
27	            if seenPoint then scale += 1 end
28	        end
29	        i += 1
30	    end
31	    if i < n then
32	        eneg = (s[i+1] = '-') OR (s[i+1] = '¯')
33	        j = if eneg OR (s[i+1] = '+') then i + 2 else i + 1 end
34	        ex := strToInt(s[j # (n - j)])
35	        if eneg then ex := -ex end
36	    end
37	    e10 = ex - scale
38	    r = if e10 >= 0 then m (10.0^e10)
39	        elif e10 >= -22 then m / (10.0^(-e10))
40	        else (m / (10.0^22)) / (10.0^(-e10 - 22)) end
41	    if neg then -r else r end
42	  end
43	
44	(* the space-separated numbers of a line, into out[off..]; returns how many *)
45	parseRow[\nat s\](line: String, out: Vector[\RR64,s\], off: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
46	    n = |line|
47	    i: ZZ32 := 0
48	    k: ZZ32 := 0
49	    while i < n do
50	        if line[i] = ' ' then i += 1
51	        else
52	            j: ZZ32 := i
53	            while (j < n) AND: (line[j] =/= ' ') do j += 1 end
54	            out[off + k] := parseFloat(line[i # (j - i)])
55	            k += 1
56	            i := j
57	        end
58	    end
59	    k
60	  end
61	(* the numbers of a line as a vector (two scans: count, then fill) *)
62	numbersOf(line: String): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
63	    cnt = parseRow(line, zeros(|line|), 0)
64	    out = zeros(cnt)
65	    parseRow(line, out, 0)
66	    out
67	  end
68	(* the lines of a file, up to the first empty one *)
69	readLines(path: String): Array[\String,ZZ32\] = do
70	    f = FileReadStream(path)
71	    cnt: ZZ32 := 0
72	    line: String := f.readLine()
73	    while |line| > 0 do cnt += 1; line := f.readLine() end
74	    f.close()
75	    g = FileReadStream(path)
76	    out = array[\String\](cnt).fill("")
77	    for i <- seq(0#cnt) do out[i] := g.readLine() end
78	    g.close()
79	    out
80	  end
81	(* one number per line *)
82	readVector(path: String, n: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
83	    f = FileReadStream(path)
84	    v = zeros(n)
85	    for i <- seq(0#n) do v[i] := parseFloat(f.readLine()) end
86	    f.close()
87	    v
88	  end
89	
90	(* the weights: files name(0) .. name(count-1) under dir, every line's numbers
91	   appended in order into one vector of `total` values -- the layout is the
92	   caller's table, the loader only concatenates *)
93	loadParams(dir: String, name: ZZ32 -> String, count: ZZ32, total: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
94	    p = zeros(total)
95	    off: ZZ32 := 0
96	    for i <- seq(0#count) do
97	        for line <- seq(readLines(dir "/" name(i) ".txt")) do off += parseRow(line, p, off) end
98	    end
99	    if off =/= total then fail("loaded " off " numbers, the layout has " total) end
100	    p
101	  end
102	
103	(* the corpus: one document per line, interned a..z; the token matrix has
104	   width block+1, BOS before and after each document and in every unused
105	   slot, and a length per document (its characters plus the leading BOS) *)
106	object Corpus(tokm: Array[\ZZ32,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\], len: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], blk: ZZ32)
107	    size(): ZZ32 = |len|
108	    length(d: ZZ32): ZZ32 = len[d]
109	    token(d: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): ZZ32 = tokm[d, j]
110	    (* the keys of a batch b of documents, one row per (document, position):
111	       the tokens at position + off, the positions, and the 0/1 validity mask *)
112	    tokens(b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], off: ZZ32): Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\] =
113	        keys(|b| blk, fn (r: ZZ32): ZZ32 => tokm[b[r DIV blk], (r MOD blk) + off])
114	    positions(b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\] =
115	        keys(|b| blk, fn (r: ZZ32): ZZ32 => r MOD blk)
116	    valid(b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] =
117	        vec(|b| blk, fn (r: ZZ32): RR64 => if (r MOD blk) < len[b[r DIV blk]] then 1.0 else 0.0 end)
118	end
119	loadCorpus(path: String, blk: ZZ32, bos: ZZ32): Corpus = do
120	    names = readLines(path)
121	    tokm = array[\ZZ32\](|names|, blk + 1).fill(bos)
122	    for d <- seq(0#|names|), j <- seq(0#|names[d]|) do tokm[d, 1 + j] := names[d][j].codePoint - 'a'.codePoint end
123	    Corpus(tokm, keys(|names|, fn (d: ZZ32): ZZ32 => 1 + |names[d]|), blk)
124	  end
125	end

1	<!-- What is established about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as it stands now, grouped by area: each entry the fact, its source and its test. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `FACTS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. -->
2	
3	# Facts on record
4	
5	## Execution model
6	
7	- F-7 **Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases, and only the compiled path runs the static type checker.** Walk switches the checker off, and no switch turns it on. So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
8	- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
9	- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled runtime"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
10	- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
11	- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
12	- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled runtime" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). The team's direction for unboxing builds on this class per instantiation (the plan in `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java`; the loader's empty "expando" stub, `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`), but a loader that stamps an `RR64` instance with a `double[]` field, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), does not exist and is unmeasured. Walk instantiates generics in its own evaluator, not by classes. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.
13	- F-19 **By the specification, the iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments of a call or an operator may run in parallel, and a program must assume that they do.** A `for` loop is sequential only if every generator is, as `seq(g)` or `sequential(g)` makes it. An implementation may also run them one after another (`evaluation/parallelism.tex:88-90`), so a program cannot count on parallel runs either. For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, the arguments of a function call and of a dotted method call fork where the analyzer marked the argument tuple (`CodeGen.evalArg`; F-350), and the analyzer marks no call written in the compiler's prelude (row 982). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits a `ZZ32` range down to chunks of `grainSize`, 16, elements, each run by the sequential range's methods, and a range with a stride down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:20`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The revival's tests under `ProjectFortress/` write both. Source: `Specification/basic/expressions/for.tex:28-32`, `tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:58-59`, `evaluation/parallelism.tex:50-80`.
14	- F-20 **Sizes, the `nat` and `int` static parameters, are values at run time; they check shapes, and no optimization uses them (F-40, what a size costs at run time).** The compiled checker checks them (F-67), and a sized program loads and runs compiled (F-129). POSITIONS.md:24
- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). 353	## 4. What the shares are, for microGPT-shaped code
354	
355	Stated plainly, and with the one caveat that governs all of it: **on the
356	compiled path, microGPT-shaped code does not run at all**, so every share below
357	that concerns the compiled path is measured on the code the compiler *can*
358	run — the fairly-written scalar loop — and on Java models of the array kernels,
359	and is labelled as such. **Boxing is a small share of the compiled path's cost
360	on the scalar loop and a large share of the representational cost in the array
361	kernels**: in the compiled Fortress ladder, everything that is left after the
362	literals and the `:=` are removed is 0.4207 s of `bench1t`'s 9.3441 s, so
363	boxing cannot exceed 4.5% of the original gap, and the Java bracket puts it
364	lower still — 0.072 s boxed against 0.043 s primitive is 0.3% of the gap, and
365	0.187 s with escape analysis defeated is 1.5%; but in the array kernels the
366	same boxes cannot be scalar-replaced, because every element result is stored
367	into an array and escapes, and there boxing costs **6.3× on the dot product,
368	6.5× on the matrix product and 2.6× on the row lift** over primitive `double[]`
369	in Java. **The transaction check is the largest single share of the compiled
370	path's cost today**, and two independent measurements agree on it: the
371	`bench1h` → `bench1r` ablation charges 5.65 s, 60.5% of `bench1t`, to removing
372	the `:=` (a bound that also contains the generator), and the Flight Recorder
373	profile of `bench1h` puts 88.9% of that run's 6.07 s — 5.40 s, 57.8% of
374	`bench1t` — under `BaseTask.inATransaction()`, most of it inside the debug
375	message the method builds before it looks at the flag that would discard it.
376	**The float-literal round-trip is 35.0%**, 3.2709 s, measured by hoisting the
377	two literals and changing nothing else, which agrees with the boxing report's
378	30% Java-model estimate; `javap` confirms the loop body no longer calls
379	`FFloatLiteral.make` or `coerce_RR64`, and the asymmetry is specific —
380	`FFloatLiteral` stores its value as a `String` and re-parses it, `FIntLiteral`
381	keeps a `long`. **Dispatch and the generic array objects are the smallest named
382	shares**: in the `bench1h` profile, closure and trait dispatch is 0.8% and
383	integer index boxing 2.3%, with the generator a further 6.3%; and in the Java
384	kernel models the generic array representation — `Object[]` behind an interface
385	with a `checkcast` on every read, plus a row-view object per row — costs only
386	**9% on `kdot`, 1.6% on `kmat` and 4.8% on `krows`** on top of boxing, so the
387	indirection is nearly free next to the allocation it holds. On the interpreter,
388	which is the only path that runs these kernels, the shares are different again
389	and none of them is representational: 43.5% AST walk, 32.3% environment
390	lookup, 5.2% run-time type dispatch, and number representation not in the
391	profile at all.
392	
393	**Where `performance-roadmap.md`'s "every `RR64` is a heap object" stands.**
394	It is true, and this probe sharpens rather than retires it — but it moves in
395	the ordering. For the scalar loop it was never the ceiling and now it is not
396	even the floor: a fairly written compiled loop is 9.7× primitive Java, and
397	boxing is at most 1.5 percentage points of the 215× it was. For array-shaped
398	code — which is what microGPT is — it is the dominant *representational* cost,
399	6.3–6.5× on the dot product and the matrix product, because array element
400	results escape and no JIT can scalar-replace them; that is the strongest
401	support the roadmap's A1/A2 (unbox by static type, `double[]`-backed arrays)
402	has had. But it is still not what makes today's numbers what they are. Today
403	the compiled path cannot express a microGPT kernel at all, and the interpreter,
404	which can, spends none of its time on representation. The order that follows
405	from this probe: first give the compiler library an `RR64` array type (G2) so
406	the kernels exist on that path at all; then the two one-line defects — the
407	`inATransaction` debug string and the `FFloatLiteral` round-trip — which
408	together are ~95% of what the compiled path currently wastes; then unboxing and
409	`double[]`, which is where the remaining 6× on array code lives, and which the
410	first step must be designed for rather than retrofitted to.

# The code generator's distance from the interpreter's library

## 0. The answers

1. **`FortressLibrary.fss` under the switch-over's setting (bound `Any`, the distance stage's default):** 504 declarations reach the declaration loop: the 500 of the source and 4 made by overload rewriting. 475 are emitted and 29 refused. 27 of the 29 are declarations the checker passed.
   - Counted as on 2026-09-27 (an object refused in the pre-pass also counts as emitted), it is 481 emitted and 29 refused, against 326 and 225.
   - Refusals on declarations the checker passed went from 4 to 27, because the checker now passes 498 of the 500 (section 2).
2. **Under the 2026-09-27 setting (the compile path's, bound `Object`):** the same file emits 460 (2026-09-27 count) and refuses 74, 15 of them on declarations the checker passed. The other 59 are on declarations the checker reports errors on under that setting, and on the overload rewrites inside them (section 2).
3. **The dispatch generator refuses no overload set, under either setting:** 0 of the 178 sets that the skipping runs pass over, against 12 of 198 on 2026-09-27. With dispatch generation on, code generation took between 35 and 65 s of a 159 s run (section 5).
4. **Over all twelve components, under the switch-over's setting, 58 declarations are refused, 50 of them on declarations the checker passed.** The other 8 lie in or under the two declarations that hold four of the distance's five errors: `__bigOperator2` and trait `List` (section 4).
5. **The 50 refusals on checked declarations fall into 14 kinds by message (table in section 3).** The largest:
   - a local function (`Can't compile LetFn`): 9 declarations, 16 local-function groups in the parsed trees;
   - "Not in the trait table" on `RangeInternals`' 2-D and 3-D range objects: 8;
   - `asif` (`Can't compile AsIfExpr`): 7 declarations, 13 sites;
   - varargs: 7. Six are `Can't compile VarArgs yet`, on a varargs parameter or a call of `assert`; one is an `OptionUnwrapException` on a varargs method;
   - a postfix operator applied to a tuple operand ("Error trying to close method scope"): 4;
   - `label`: 3.

   Rows 304, 81, 315, 540, 624, 701 and 733 hold kinds. Row 650 holds the modifier guard, for `override` only. Six forms have no row:
   - `asif`;
   - the tuple-operand postfix operator;
   - the static argument `Any` in an `extends` clause;
   - `forbid`;
   - "is not in the kind env" in the code generator;
   - the `test` modifier.

## 1. How it was measured

- **Machine**: `nproc` 4; Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz, `cpu MHz` 2100.000; JDK `openjdk version "25.0.4.1" 2026-08-18`; `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`; `-Xmx4g -Xss64m`.
  - Every JVM ran under `nice -n 19`, one at a time, beside a climb batch.
  - Load average at the runs' starts: 2.25 to 7.20. No timing here is a comparison.
- **Tree**: worktree `/home/user/fortress-cgdist`, detached at `main`'s `aa5c67d48`, seeded from `/home/user/fortress-base21b` (`24919e97d`). `git diff --stat 24919e97d aa5c67d48 -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml bin` prints nothing, so the base build's classes are `main`'s code.
- **Shadows**: `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/shadow-patch.py` and `add-patch.py`, the distance stage's copies.
  - They are byte-identical to the 2026-09-27 probe's `desugar-codegen/shadow-patch.py` and `switch-over-distance/add-patch.py`: `git show fc89ee7a5^:<path>`, then `diff`, prints nothing.
  - They write shadow copies of `StaticChecker`, `TypeCheckPhase`, `DesugarPhase`, `CodeGenerationPhase`, `CodeGen`, `Desugarer` and `NodeComparator`. javac compiles them into a scratch folder put ahead of `ProjectFortress/build` on the class path. Every edit matched today's sources.
  - Under `-Dprobe.tolerant` the checker checks each top-level declaration apart, and its errors do not stop the run.
  - Code generation catches each failure in four places: `CodeGen`'s constructor (inherited methods), dispatch generation, the object and variable pre-pass, and the declaration loop. After a catch it restores the loop's declaration state.
- **Drivers**:
  - the 2026-09-27 `Distance.java` (`git show fc89ee7a5^:explorations/perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance/Distance.java`), for the compile path's setting and the compiler's prelude;

The distance stage now runs `any` by default: the setting the switch-over takes under answer (a) of batch 7's Q1 (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`, header). So `any` is the main run here, and `compile` is the like-for-like repeat.
- **Classifier**: the 2026-09-27 `desugar-codegen/classify.py`, with three changes:

- **Controls**:

1	# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code
2	
3	**seeding**
4	: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
5	
6	**base build**
7	: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.
8	
9	**old code**
10	: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.
11	
12	Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.
13	
14	## Finding or building a base build
15	
16	- If your brief names a base build, use it.
17	- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
18	  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
19	  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
20	  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
21	- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.
22	
23	      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
24	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
25	      ant compileAll
26	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
27	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
28	      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean
29	
30	If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.
31	
32	## Seeding a worktree
33	
34	A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.
35	
36	Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.
37	
38	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
39	
40	- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
41	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
42	- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
43	- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
44	- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
45	- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
46	- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
47	- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.
48	
49	## Running the old code
50	
51	If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.
52	
53	`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
54	
55	    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
56	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
57	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
58	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
59	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM
60	
61	- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
62	- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
63	- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
64	- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).
65	
66	To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:
67	
68	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
69	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
70	
71	The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
72

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's distance stage: the compiled checker over the whole interpreter library, the
# fourteen components, the prelude's twelve and the two that List imports, and their apis,
# every stage of every unit run whatever the earlier stages reported, so that nothing hides
# behind an early return; one table.
#
# Why it exists: Pavol's answer 11 (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-26): the full measurement of the
# distance to the switch-over "becomes a report-only stage of phase 3's gates, whose job is
# driving it down". The checker-count stage beside it (../checker-count/run.sh) sees only
# the errors before each api's early return, 62 of about 1,740 on 2026-09-27.
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched: the
# shadow sources and classes, the driver, the checker's caches (-Dfortress.caches) and the
# JVM's temporary directory (so Rats! leaves nothing in /tmp) go to the scratch directory
# (default: $TMPDIR or /tmp), and the caches are deleted at the end. It never removes
# /tmp/fortress*rats, which other runs on the machine use. Exit 0 if the table was
# produced, 1 if it could not be. One JVM, -Xmx4g, one busy core: 789 s on the idle 4-CPU
# container on 2026-09-27, 14 to 24 minutes under load 7 to 18 (switch-over-distance-flat.md
# section 5); the table's #seconds and #machine rows say what each run took and where.
#
# The setting: "compile" by default, the compile command's own: DistanceMulti's -setting
# compile takes the extends-Object pre-desugaring from the line that opens
# Shell.useCompilerLibraries() in the tracked ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java,
# read at each run (the run stops, with no total, if that line is not there; its "### order="
# line prints the switch it read, extendsObject=...), and turns the compiled-expression
# desugaring on, as the compile path does. Answer 11 names the compile path's setting. That
# line sets the switch off, the implicit bound Any of P-42 (row 412), so the default runs as
# "any", which fixes the switch off whatever Shell.java says; with the switch on, the compile
# setting gave 685 errors on climb batch 22's code, 580 on the bound Object (F-289). "any"
# differs from walk's setting by the compiled-expression desugaring: on the tree of 2026-09-27
# 1,746 to 1,747 errors against 1,737 to 1,738 (FACTS.md, "The true distance to the
# switch-over"). The third argument, any or walk, runs another setting, for a comparison
# with the measurements on file; the gate never passes it.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false), as in
# every run of the measurement: keyed on declaration pairs, it hides 27 to 35 errors
# depending on the build order (FACTS.md, "The overloading checker's memo hides errors
# by build order, so every count runs with it off ...").
#
# The sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-27, so that the gate does not
# depend on a probe directory, as the checker-count stage's were: DistanceMulti.java from
# perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat/ (35ef70584); shadow-patch.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen/ (e5d8cdbd2); add-patch.py and errors.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance/ (a7e3df9ad, 14d2f9839); classify.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage/ (e17a9badc); all unchanged but classify.py, which since
# row 577 finds the library places that name three of its classes by their declarations in
# the tree's sources ($FH, passed to table.py), not by line ranges. table.py is new: it
# counts as those scripts count and prints the rows below. The shadow classes are not
# copies: they are made from the tracked sources at every run by text edits that must each
# match exactly once (shadow-patch.py, add-patch.py), so there is no copied checker to go
# stale silently; an edit that no longer matches stops the run before the checker starts,
# and the table then says so in its #shadow row, with no counts.
#
# The table, tab-separated, every row tagged:
#   #distance   the setting, the switches and the fourteen targets
#   #total      distinct errors; or "none:" and why, when no total was measured, as when a
#               target stopped with errors the stage does not count, such as a parse error,
#               or an api that only a later target checks reported errors (table.py)
#   #kind       by kind (errors.py): exclusion, comprises, overloading, return-type, ...
#   #class      by root cause (classify.py, distance-triage.md section 2), with its name
#   #check      a disagreement: errors.py's and table.py's totals, or sites classify.py cannot
#               find in the tree's library source
#   #unit       by the unit that printed the error first
#   #crash      each declaration, stage or target the checker crashed on
#   #seconds    the run's wall time, and FortressLibrary's, the part that takes it
#   #machine    nproc, CPU model and MHz, load at start, JDK, FORTRESS_THREADS
#   #shadow     whether every shadow edit matched the tracked sources; the last row
# ../distance/compare.sh compares two tables. The run-to-run variation is 2 to 4 errors,
# in the comparisons' and Maybe's pairs and the joins of array bodies (switch-over-
# distance-flat.md section 5).
set -u
#    steps), and the driver; a text edit that no longer matches is the one way this can go stale
SHADOW="every shadow edit matched the tracked sources"
if ! ( cd "$FH" && python3 "$D/shadow-patch.py" ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" \
                && python3 "$D/add-patch.py" "$SCRATCH/shadow-src" ) > "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" 2>&1 ; then
    SHADOW="STALE: a shadow edit no longer matches the tracked sources: $(grep -E '^AssertionError' "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" | tail -1 | tr -s ' ' | cut -c1-200); see $SCRATCH/shadows.txt"
elif ! javac -nowarn -encoding UTF-8 -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/shadow-classes" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/TypeCheckPhase.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/DesugarPhase.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/CodeGenerationPhase.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Desugarer.java" \
        "$SCRATCH/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/NodeComparator.java" >> "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" 2>&1 ; then
    SHADOW="STALE: the shadow sources no longer compile against the tree; see $SCRATCH/shadows.txt"
elif ! javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/classes" "$D/DistanceMulti.java" >> "$SCRATCH/shadows.txt" 2>&1 ; then
    SHADOW="STALE: DistanceMulti.java no longer compiles against the tree; see $SCRATCH/shadows.txt"
fi

# 2. the run: one JVM, the fourteen components, FortressLibrary first so that its run checks
#    the apis that it imports, at any depth, with every stage (DistanceMulti.java's header);
#    an api that only a later target imports, as OneShotFlag's, is checked as the tracked
#    method checks it and prints only its count, which table.py reads
RC=
case "$SHADOW" in
  STALE*) : > "$SCRATCH/run.txt" ;;
  *) S=$(date +%s)
     ( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 30 5400 java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow \
           -Djava.io.tmpdir="$SCRATCH/tmp" -Dfortress.caches="$SCRATCH/caches" $FLAGS \
           -cp "$SCRATCH/shadow-classes:$SCRATCH/classes:$CP" DistanceMulti -order check -setting "$SETTING" $COMPONENTS
     ) > "$SCRATCH/run.txt" 2>&1
     RC=$? ; ELAPSED=$(( $(date +%s) - S ))
     rm -rf "$SCRATCH/caches" "$SCRATCH/tmp" ;;
esac

# 3. the table. errors.py's tally and its one-row-per-error list stay in the scratch
#    directory for whoever needs the sites (compare-sites, the review); table.py's rows go
#    into the table, and their total is checked against errors.py's own count.
{
    printf '#distance\tsetting %s; %s; %s\n' "$SETTING" "$FLAGS" "$(echo $COMPONENTS | wc -w) components in one JVM (DistanceMulti -order check)"
    if grep -q '^### all seconds=' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" ; then
        python3 -B "$D/table.py" "$SCRATCH/run.txt" "$FH" > "$SCRATCH/rows.txt" 2>&1
        cat "$SCRATCH/rows.txt"
        python3 "$D/errors.py" "$SCRATCH/errors.tsv" "$SCRATCH/run.txt" > "$SCRATCH/tally.txt" 2>&1
        E=$(sed -n 's/^# \([0-9]*\) distinct errors.*/\1/p' "$SCRATCH/tally.txt")
        T=$(awk -F'\t' '$1 == "#total" { print $2 }' "$SCRATCH/rows.txt")
        case "$T" in none*) ;; *)
        [ "$E" = "$T" ] || printf '#check\terrors.py counts %s, table.py %s: the two normalisations differ on this run; see %s\n' "$E" "$T" "$SCRATCH/tally.txt" ;; esac
        printf '#seconds\t%s\tFortressLibrary %s\n' "${ELAPSED:-?}" "$(sed -n 's/^### done Library\/FortressLibrary.fss rc=-\{0,1\}[0-9]* seconds=\([0-9]*\)$/\1/p' "$SCRATCH/run.txt")"
    else
        case "$SHADOW" in
          STALE*) printf '#total\tnone: the checker did not run\n' ;;
          *) printf '#total\tnone: the run ended without its last line (rc=%s); see %s\n' "${RC:-?}" "$SCRATCH/run.txt" ;;
        esac
    fi
    printf '#machine\t%s\n' "$MACHINE"
    printf '#shadow\t%s\n' "$SHADOW"
} > "$OUT"

cat "$OUT"
echo "# distance: full output $SCRATCH/run.txt, rc=${RC:-not run}; errors.py's tally $SCRATCH/tally.txt"
grep -q '^#total	[0-9]' "$OUT"

1	# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
2	
3	**tree**
4	: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.
5	
6	**library order**
7	: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
8	
9	**DSL grammar**
10	: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.
11	
12	**parser directory**
13	: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.
14	
15	## Setting up each call
16	
17	Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:
18	
19	    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
20	    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
21	    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
22	    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
23	
24	- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
25	- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
26	- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.
27	
28	The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:
29	
30	- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
31	- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).
32	
33	If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.
34	
35	The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.
36	
37	With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:
38	
39	- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
40	- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.
41	
42	## Two layers of code
43	
44	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
45	
46	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
47	
48	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
49	
50	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
51	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
52	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
53	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
54	
55	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
56	
57	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
58	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
59	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
60	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
61	
62	## The caches
63	
64	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
65	
66	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
67	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
68	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
69	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
70	
71	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
72	
73	## The library order
74	
75	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
76	
77	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
78	
79	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
80	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
81	
82	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
83	
84	    cd ProjectFortress
85	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
86	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
87	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
88	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
89	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
90	
91	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
92	
93	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
94	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
95	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
96	
97	## Name resolution
98	
99	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
100	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
101	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
102	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
103	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
104	
105	## Building
106	
107	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
108	
109	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
110	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
111	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
112	- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
113	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
114	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
115	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
116	
117	## After an edit of the library
118	
119	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
120	
121	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
122	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
123	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
124	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
125	
126	## Symptoms of a skipped step
127	
128	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
129	
130	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
131	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
132	
133	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
134	
135	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
136	
137	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
138	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
139	
140	Two more facts help you read a run:
141	
142	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
143	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.

import re,collections
txt=open('tmp/p1/c4/run.txt').read().replace('/home/user/fortress-planrev/','')
seen=collections.OrderedDict()
for m in re.finditer(r'@@SC ERR\tcomponent (\S+)\t(\S+)\t(\S+?):(\d+):(\S+?): +(.*)', txt):
    comp,stage,f,line,col,msg=m.groups()
    key=(comp,f,line,col.split('-')[0],msg[:60])
    seen.setdefault(key,(stage,msg))
by=collections.Counter(k[0] for k in seen)
print(by)
for k,(st,msg) in seen.items():
    if k[0] in('FileSupport',): continue
    print(k[0],k[2]+':'+k[3],st,'|',msg[:170])
EOF

<!-- A reminder for the curator, 2026-11-10, of what is on file about arrays, matrix computation and parallel splitting; read only, nothing run. -->

# Arrays, matrix products and parallel splitting: what is on file

Paths are under `explorations/` unless they start with `Library/`, `Specification/`, `ProjectFortress/` or `research/`. `FL.fss` is `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`. `RI.fss` is `Library/RangeInternals.fss`.

## 1. What the sizes in the types buy

A `nat` is a size that a type carries. A case (`FL.fss:3192-3193`):

    opr DOT[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat n, nat m\]
           (me: Matrix[\T,n,m\], v: Vector[\T,m\]): Vector[\T,n\] = me.rmul(v)

The one `m` ties the matrix's columns to the vector's length. A 27 by 16 matrix times a 16-vector checks. Times a 27-vector, the compile stops.

**Measured** (`perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md`, "The answers" and section 5):

- The checker refuses a wrong size once, at the call site, at compile time. A call that the checker resolved tests no size when it runs.
- A call chosen at run time by size costs 4 to 20 ns more than a resolved one.
- Inside a class made for size 8, the size is the constant 8 in the bytecode. A loop bounded by that constant was not measurably faster than a loop bounded by the store's length read at run time.
- "Nothing today builds an optimisation on a size."
- The measured cost is boxing, a number kept as an object: in Java models of microGPT's kernels, 6.3 times (dot product), 6.5 ti

<!-- What Pavol, the curator, knows, graded by topic, for pitching an explanation or an ask at him, with each line's evidence in PROFILE-sources.md beside it. -->

# What Pavol knows

A topic reads `topic — level — how to pitch it`. `1 → 3` is a level that rose: pitch at the later one.

- 4, expert: hands-on depth; talk as to a peer.
- 3, working: uses it correctly; no explanation, define only the project's own terms.
- 2, familiar: knows the idea, not the details; a one-line reminder before it is used.
- 1, heard of: knows the name; explain it with one concrete case before using it.
- 0, new: explain from the ground up, concrete cases first, with the shortest grounding that worked where there is one.

## Topics

### Languages and tools

- Benchmarking and measurement statistics — 4 — talk as to a peer; frame speed results this way.
- Swift as a library and benchmark writer — 3 — his first frame; its compiler's insides, and its names for unique references and copy-on-write, are 1.
- Scala (2.8 era), Java and the JVM, Python, iOS, as a user — 3 — take as known; their compilers' insides are new.
- Rust, Julia, Kotlin, Clojure, C++ templates — 2 — one line on the peer's idea; Clojure's multimethods are 1.
- What generators cost against a loop — 3 — he measured it himself; use it for big operators.
- APL — 0 — the side quest is closed.

### Types and language design

- Type theory, formally — 0 — a concrete Fortress program and several cases before any rule.
- Dispatch on all arguments; exclusions; coercion against subtyping; `Any` against `Object` — 1 → 3 — take as known.
- The checker's overload rules — 1 — the idea stuck, the rules didn't; show concrete pairs of declarations.
- Erased against kept generics; traits that give behavior; a subtype with its own operation — 3 — he judges by ergonomics and reuse, not purity.
- `where` clauses; soundness — 0 → 2 — remind him that `where` narrows where a declaration applies.
- `nat` size parameters — 0 → 2 — remind him that a `nat` is a size the type carries; arithmetic on sizes is 0.
- An interface against a trait — 1 — he is unsure of the words; say "extends".

### Mathematics

- Matrix and vector products, the dot product — 1 — he knows only that inner dimensions match; start from a 2×2 matrix times a vector, show that order matters, then C4's shapes: 16×16 (attention), 27×16 (token table), 64×16 (feed-forward).
- Rings, fields, additive groups — 0 — no grounding has worked yet.
- Identity elements on each type's algebra — 3 — take as known.
- Q, Z and N; `ZZ` signed, `NN` not — 0 → 3 — take as known.
- The library's number types — 2 — bottom up, `ZZ32` first; top down failed.
- Floating point — 2 — he knows IEEE rounding against Java's; infinities among the rationals were new.
- Reshape, ravel, outer product, tensor — 0 — define each on a small array.
- Mathematical notation — 1 — set it beside the Fortress code that computes it.

### Machine learning

- micrograd, microGPT, nanoGPT; FP32; integer tokens — 3 — take as known; microGPT's baseline is CPython or NumPy.
- KV cache, loss curves, early stopping, Chinchilla — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- Backpropagation, functional or tape-style, and its cost — 1 — his views are guesses.
- Big operators as ML papers write them — 1 — "hardly a yardstick", he says.
- Attention and softmax — 0 — learning them was microGPT's point for him; teach from C4's code.

### Fortress, its sources and the record

- Steele's talks: juxtaposition, undefined precedence, parallel loops, inference, units, `Σ` over new types — 3 — take as known.
- Where intent lives: the papers, the TeX not the PDF, the team's later word, the library among the sources — 3 — his rules.
- Who did what: Ryu's front end, Park's POPL 2019 paper — 3 — take as known.
- The library's shape: `Vector` and `Matrix` for numbers only — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The specification, the papers, the library's text — 1 — unread; quote the line that decides.
- Reading Fortress code — 1 → 2 — he reads a declaration line by line; gloss each new construct.
- `label` and `exit`, `comprises`, `atomic`, `thrower`, `reflect`, DSL blocks, where whitespace counts — 0 — one concrete case each.
- FACTS, POSITIONS, the original protocol — 0 — never read; say what an entry says.
- Walk against the compiled path; the compiler's prelude — 0 → 3 — take as known.

### Compilers and run times

- JVM performance: boxing, the JIT, specialization, unboxed doubles — 1 → 3 — where he grew most.
- The pipeline, the caches, JVM array limits, warm-up, races hidden by one thread — 3 — take as known.
- Loom, the Vector API, Truffle, GraalVM — 0 → 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The class loader and its descriptors — 0 → 2 — from his own picture: sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names, so the JIT drops bounds checks.
- One-time facts: which phases run the checker, the earlier compiler, a coercion's cost at run time, a load of 30 — 1 — one line when it comes up.
- The checker count and the distance to the switch-over — 1 — each time: what each counts, and why one can jump.

### The repository and the process

- Git; Claude Code's client; test-first, with `XXX` tests until a fix flips them — 3 — take as known.
- The platform: remote sessions, secrets in a container, the weekly reset — 1 — one line when it matters.
- The project's own terms; his past rulings — 2 — he forgets them after a gap; restate them by content.
- POSITIONS, "History he knows", and his decisions — 3 — take as known; cite a decision by what it says, never by its number.
- The coordinator's three principles — 1 — he knows the nine-step form, not these.

## How to explain to him

- Pitch at a software engineer who directs the work, not a researcher. Say what a feature costs.
- Concrete cases before the rule: several, on C4 or a Fortress program. He checks them for a contradiction, then takes the rule.
- Frame in what he knows, his own analogies first: the complex-number Mandelbrot, the diagonal matrix, Swift's debug builds, LLVM's lit.
- Define each term where it is used.
- Show Fortress code as Fortress, infix, not calls. Set notation beside the code. Draw a picture where structure matters.
- An ask: the question, context with a primer, numbered options with trade-offs and none that does nothing, the ask, the recommendation last. On types: the specification and the team's later word first, then the library, then the peers as context only. Say what each option does for a fast microGPT.
- One ask at a time, answerable as "3b". Show the wording before a yes. Mark a decision surfaced for his learning as one.
- Length by mode: three lines and "holding" while he reads turn by turn; an ask 1.5K to 3.3K, 5K with a refresher; long only to establish facts, never unasked.
- If he answers a long turn piece by piece: hold, list his points, and wait.
- When he's tired: one item, a default he can take, an offer to come back to it.
- When he ends "how wrong am I?": answer it, and reflect his idea back refined.
- He reads fast and forgets: restate, don't refer back.
- Plain words, halfway to ASD-STE100, positive phrasing.
- The phone, with Speak: a Select button per section, links not paths, no tables, numbers as K and M. A stop can be an accidental tap.
- Dictation: repair a term silently unless two readings differ. Seen, as heard → meant: forty five → Fortify, contact → compact, WordPress → Fortress, Table → Fable, scalar → Scala, Perl → parallel, Docker → checker, time system → type system, rank → rung, net → nat, Sue → Hsu, Popple → POPL, 16 → 64.

## Words to avoid

- A bare label: "P1", "row 40", "answer 9", "the judge", "the line". Name the thing.
- "Closure" for the integer tower; "sealed" for `Σ`; "revising the specification" for reconciling its contradictions.
- "Tensor", "reshape", "ravel", "outer product", "ring", "field", undefined; "coercion" for "conversion".
- "Yesterday"; "we" for him and Claude; a coda, a slogan, a clever turn.

## Open contradictions

- Length: he demands short replies, yet praised a long one while facts were being established.
- Reading: he says he hasn't read the specification or the library, yet spot-checks them and recalls Steele's talks exactly.
- Type theory: he says he knows none, yet reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure.
- Scala: he says it earned his Stack Overflow points; most of the account is iOS.
- Peers: he asks what they do, yet rules that they only decide between the designers' choices; "context only" is the record's reading.
- Ownership: he wants every choice, yet at times takes a default unread.
- History: he recalls `main` as free of the third-party port; the record says otherwise.
- Other languages: his claims about them are unchecked; check one before building on it.
